info.bio:
Cecil Bustamente Campbell (nacido el 28 de mayo de 1938), más conocido como Prince Buster, es un músico musulmán de Kingston, Jamaica, y es recordado como una de las máximas figuras del ska y el rocksteady. Sus discos en el sello Blue Beat en los 60 han inspirado a multitud de cantantes de reggae y ska.

[Más en la Wikipedia]

scenes.name: El soul conquista Gran Bretaña
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: El 26 de octubre «Reach Out I’ll Be There» de los Four Tops, con la flauta de aire oriental, el fraseo dylaniano de Lamont Dozier y la interpretación de su vida de Levi Stubbs, desbancó a «Distant Drums» y fue número 1: el momento en que la música negra americana ocupó el centro de la cultura juvenil británica, al revés que en el boom del beat. Lo habían preparado durante años los entusiastas: Dave Godin, que fundó en 1963 la Tamla Motown Appreciation Society, viajó a Detroit, llevó «Where Did Our Love Go» a los piratas y bautizó el sello Tamla Motown (marzo de 1965, con una gira de la revista que fracasó fuera de Londres); Guy Stevens, que pinchaba discos negros en el Scene y dirigió Sue Records para Chris Blackwell; Roger Eagle en el Twisted Wheel de Mánchester; Tony Hall promocionando Atlantic («In the Midnight Hour», el «My Girl» de Otis Redding); el DJ Jeff Dexter mezclando soul y ska en Tiles, el club subterráneo de Oxford Street del mod de masas que visitó Tom Wolfe. En otoño de 1966 Atlantic y Motown copaban las listas; Otis Redding metió a 8.000 personas en Tiles; los Four Tops arrasaron en el Savile de Brian Epstein el 13 de noviembre. El racismo, aun así, seguía ahí.

scenes.name: Ska y rocksteady en Londres
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Savage dejó fuera el ska por la casi imposibilidad de fechar los discos, pero estaba en todas partes: Peter Meaden veía en 1964 un movimiento mod que solo tenía pop americano, R&B y «una pizca de ska jamaicano»; Island editó desde 1963 una avalancha de ska y Chris Blackwell diversificó con Sue; en Le Duce y en Tiles sonaban Prince Buster, Desmond Dekker o los Wailers, y en Tiles el ska llegó a dominar: «cualquiera podía bailar un disco de ska», y por primera vez la juventud negra se mezclaba en los clubes. La discografía del libro recoge algunos sencillos del año.

scenes.name: Ska jamaicano y soul de los sesenta
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: El ska, «R&B dado vuelta», nace a finales de los cincuenta; Prince Buster, su supuesto inventor, era aún más conocido en Inglaterra, donde los mods lo escoltaban en motoneta. Los mods originales que no se pasaron a la psicodelia se hicieron skinheads amantes del ska y el rocksteady o fans del Motown y el northern soul («a mí me gusta la música para bailar, no escuchar»). Geno Washington y su Ram Jam Band, el soul de Stax y Atlantic: el repertorio que 2-Tone y Dexys recuperan.

scenes.name: Reggae y dub
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El reggae se populariza en el Reino Unido con Prince Buster y Desmond Dekker; Jimmy Cliff lo casa con el «paz y amor» hippy y los Maytals le dan nombre. Los sound systems de los guetos convierten a los «selectors» en los verdaderos animadores: el «toasting» sobre los discos será tan importante como la música. Bob Marley y los Wailers lo llevan a Occidente; Burning Spear firma quizá su cima artística (Marcus Garvey). Los ingenieros remezclan las caras B quitando las voces: King Tubby inventa el dub usando la mesa de mezclas como un instrumento, y Lee Perry (Super Ape) y Augustus Pablo fijan el canon.

mentions.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
mentions.author: Simon Reynolds
mentions.text: …más lentos, inocentes y simples que los remakes. 331 El hombre al que, generalmente, se considera el inventor del ritmo ska, el cantante y productor Prince Buster, era aún más conocido en Inglaterra que en Jamaica. Lanzó más de seiscientos singles en el Reino Unido entre 1962 y 1967, y estaba constantemente de gira, donde lo solían escoltar mods en motoneta entre show y show. The Specials respetaba esta tradicional devoción por Buster. Por ejemplo, "Gangster" se basa libremente en su tema ''Al Capone", reemplazando las letras originales con referencias a los empresarios y abogados…

mentions.text: …Matón), que condena con duras sentencias a un grupo de rude boys) toma prestada su ambientación judicial de "Judge Oread" [Juez Terror), un hit de Buster de 1967. podcast.title: Death (September 9, 2016)
podcast.body: Prince Buster, a renowned pioneer of ska music, died on September 9, 2016, due to a stroke. "September 9th, Prince Buster, a great scop pioneer, a stroke."

podcast.title: Assistant to Coxsone Dodd
podcast.body: Prince Buster initially worked for Coxsone Dodd as an assistant, running one of Dodd's many sound systems. He later became a significant figure in his own right. "Like Prince Buster and Lee Scratch Perry."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Black Nationalist and Rastafari Adherent
podcast.body: Prince Buster was a staunch black nationalist and a follower of the Rastafari religion. This conviction fueled his desire to create a purely Jamaican music, distinguishing him from rivals like Dodd and Reid who viewed their productions as R&B substitutes. "Vince Buster, on the other hand, by this point was a full-fledged black nationalist and wanted to make a purely Jamaican music. Buster was, in particular, an adherent of the Rastafar Avalidium."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Early Practitioner of Ska
podcast.body: Prince Buster is identified as one of the early practitioners of ska, a local sound originating in Jamaica. His cover of a 1949 song in 1963 demonstrates his involvement in the early development and popularization of the genre. "In 1963, it was covered by Prince Buster, one of the early practitioners of a local sound called ska."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Establishing Own Sound System
podcast.body: Eventually, Prince Buster left Coxsone Dodd to set up his own rival sound system, escalating the soundman rivalry into a three-way competition in Kingston. "Eventually Prince Buster left Dodd and set up his own rival sound system, at which point the rivalry became a three way one."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Incorporating Rasta Rhythms into Ska
podcast.body: For his single "O'Carolina," Prince Buster brought in five drummers from the Rasta Nyabinghi tradition, including the influential Count Ossie. This marked the first time Rasta's sacred music rhythms were integrated into Jamaican R&B, contributing to Ska's development. "he brought in five drummers from the Rasta Niabinghi tradition, most notably Count Osie, who became the single most influential drummer in Jamaica, to record on the folks for the single O'Carolina, incorporating the rhythms of Rasta's sacred music into Jamaican R&B for the first time."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Patois Quote on Dodd's Reaction
podcast.body: Prince Buster famously described Coxsone Dodd's psychological collapse when Duke Reid played "Gator" by Willis Gatortail Jackson, using Jamaican Patois to convey the moment. The quote illustrates the intensity of the soundman rivalry. "The psychological impact had knocked him out, nobody never hit him."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: R&B Espionage for Dodd
podcast.body: Prince Buster possessed a deep knowledge of R&B, enabling him to attend Duke Reid's shows, identify the production styles of different R&B labels, and use lyrics to deduce the titles and labels of Reed's exclusive records. This information was then used by Dodd to obtain copies and undermine Reid's competitive edge. "one important one being that he knew enough about R&B, that he could go to Duke Reed's shows, listen to the records he was playing, and figure out what they must be."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Showmanship Prowess
podcast.body: In the competitive sound system scene, Prince Buster was recognized as the best showman. He understood what his audience desired and expertly delivered it, making his shows immensely popular. "Prince Buster was the best showman, who knew what the people wanted and gave it to them."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Ska Giant and Saxa's Collaborator
podcast.body: Prince Buster is recognized as a "Ska Giant" with whom The English Beat's saxophonist, Saxa, had previously played in his early career. "saxo had played with Scott Giants like Prince Buster and Desmond Decker in the early days, so this guy really knew what he was doing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Co-writer of a 1949 Song
xref.body: Carl Sigmund co-wrote a song in 1949 with Herb Madison. This song was later recorded by Guy Lombardo and Canadians in 1950, becoming a hit, and then covered by Bing Crosby, Doris Day, Prince Buster, and The Specials. "Those are the specials covering a song from 1949 written by Americans Carl Sigmund and Herb Madison at a time when Trag Jazz was happening in the US."

xref.title: Madness – Named After Old Prince Buster Song; North London Group; "Nutty Sound"
xref.body: Madness was a North London group with what was described as a "nutty sound" — a loose blend of punk and traditional Jamaican ska. Two-Tone signed them and issued their first singles. Their name came from an old Prince Buster song called "Madness." "Two-tone also issued the first singles from a group that featured Prince Buster's old saxophone player, and they were called Mbiet." [Madness]
